utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. If the registrar would be so kind as to call out the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-95-13a-T, the Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dokmanovic, do you feel comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, yesterday we left off with -- at Vodicka. Could you tell me who Zlatko and Jovanka Vodicka were, how did you come to know them, make friends with them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to apologise for what happened yesterday, first of all. I was emotionally very close to that man, and I was very distressed. Zlatko Vodicka was my best friend. I've known him since 1971. Jovanka came in 1972. We were together almost every single day, and he died on the 15th of September last year, and that is why I was so distressed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were in prison at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was Zlatko Vodicka by nationality and how did he declare himself and what religion was he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: He declared himself as a Croat of the Catholic faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how as a Catholic, if his father was a Czech and his mother an Austrian?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, his parents were also born in the territory of Croatia and his parents always declared themselves as Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should like to ask you now, if I may, to explain once again whether, at that time, on the 20th of November at VELEPROMET, you learned something of the fate of Jovanka and Zlatko and what happened to them generally in the war situation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Zlatko was at my house and Jovanka was in the basement, in the cellar in Vukovar because they had a house in Vukovar. He went to look for her on the 18th; that is to say, when entrance to Vukovar was possible. I did not know what was happening, but on the 18th he did not find her. He went again on the 19th and then he found Jovanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you learn of this and when?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I learned of this in VELEPROMET from Kosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is to say on the 20th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 20th. Because Zlatko, when he found Jovanka as he found her near Sid on the motorway, he went -- they slept in Sid and stayed in Sid and Kosic's family was in Sid, and somehow or other they saw each other and they said -- he said that Zlatko had found Jovanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we see the tape at one particular point when you say -- say something, a sentence. Could you tell us -- it is D2? Could you tell us what the sentence is, what you are saying in that sentence? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you say there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I said Zlatko has found Jovanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that refer to Vodicka?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was for me a very happy piece of news because we had lost all hope, both Zlatko and us, we thought that Jovanka had perhaps died in the fighting around Vukovar because he had heard nothing of her for almost a month, he didn't know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before he came to your house to live, Zlatko Vodicka, in what town did he live?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Zlatko Vodicka was a veterinary (sic), and they lived in Vukovar where they had their family house, they lived in Trpinja for some 15 years in the veterinary station, in the flat above it. After that they built a house in Vukovar and moved to Vukovar sometime after 1980, I think, perhaps '83, '84, but Zlatko continued to work in Trpinja as a vet. Jovanka worked in the veterinary station in Vukovar. At the time when Vukovar was closed off and nobody was able to leave Vukovar and the villages around were closed off Zlatko could no longer travel to Trpinja, and then they transferred him to work at Jakobovac which is a livestock farm near Vukovar. And he worked there for some time, I think somewhere until the 15th or 16th of October, when Vukovar was closed off, when the army set up a blockade at Vukovar from that direction, he was at work, at Jakobovac on the farm and he was not able to return to Vukovar. The only free road, passable road, was towards Ilok, so he went to Ilok. Jovanka remained in Vukovar, and from that day they had no contact. They did not hear each other or see each other until they were reunited again on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is to say, when -- when you were left -- when they left Ilok. Did Markovic, the President of the Municipality, did he invite you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I got a message the day before saying Zlatko had asked me to wait. I did not know that he was in Ilok because we were not in contact, so that on that day, I went there to see. I thought it was that day. However, it turned out not to be that day but the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which means that you went to Ilok twice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you on the bridge the first day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ljuba Novakovic was there, I came to him in the municipal building to see what was going on and they told me that he was on the bridge so I went to the bridge and asked what was happening there, and they said that the next day Ilok would be evacuated and I remained there some five or ten minutes and returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then you went back the next day and then you met Vodicka and that is how he came to be in your house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should now like to ask for the tape, the last minute, 15.42, the time 15.42 p.m. Could you tell me if you hear your voice and tell us what you are saying and where you're saying it? (Videotape played). Mr. Dokmanovic, was that your voice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please -- may we rewind the tape? When you hear your voice, please say that it is you speaking and tell us what you were saying. May we have the tape again, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those are Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you say there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I said a sentence -- well, they're really fucking me and how come they would have to know me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that from Negoslavci and on the turning -- as we can see that Mr. Bos has returned, may we show the accused Exhibit D48?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is my clothing. I wore that clothing on the 20th of November, 1991, but also I had it before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, sometime in June, you left Vukovar. Could you tell us what you wore from June up to the 21st of November and later on, 1991, and why you wore what you wore?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer, I wore jeans and a T-shirt. At times I would wear something else, change into something else, depending on the conditions prevailing, and in the autumn I began to wear this clothing when it became colder. I had a greenish jacket from the Vupik Vukovar company that we received as workers, and the jacket, when it was cold, that was the jacket that I wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why did you wear this clothing in the wintertime?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, autumn, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were at least two reasons. The first reason was a practical reason because it was easier to maintain this type of clothing, compared to classical suits and classical clothes. In view of the conditions we lived in, no electricity, water only from time to time, everything had to be washed by hand. And the other reason was that the times were such that civilians were -- that people didn't like to see civilians so much, that it was better to wear clothing of this kind for passing through checkpoints. That was the situation. Civilians were at a disadvantage. So practically everybody wore some kind of uniform, and anybody not in some kind of uniform would be the odd man out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, you said that you recognised on the tape the last sequence because between Vukovar and Negoslavci, on the road, there are no houses at that time, there were no houses. I'm going to show you a tape which is the exhibit of the Prosecution, P28, and I think that it is item 14, it is a picture taken by the Prosecution from a helicopter. They seem to have far more sophisticated means than I do, so it is better to see the evidence provided by the Prosecution. Can any houses be seen in that picture? Would you say whether it is found -- it is found that from Vukovar to Negoslavci, there are no houses where the buses were? May we see the tape, please? That's Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now pay attention, please. Not 3. Fourteen, please. You can start with 13 and go on to 14. In the meantime, while we set technical matters right, I am going to ask you the last question of this investigation. Are you married? Do you have a family? How did you get married? Tell us a little bit about yourself while we're seeing to the tape.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I am married to a wonderful woman, I've been married since 1969. We have two grown-up children, a daughter, who is married, and a son, who is married.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you have any grandchildren?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have two grandchildren, a little girl, she's 8 years old, whom you saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: And a boy of eight months.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Whom, unfortunately, you have not seen yet. And your daughter is expecting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my daughter is expecting a third baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you ever convicted of any crime in your life?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I was a court expert for many years, I had no problems when it came to law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Apart from the love of your family, what other -- what else can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I come from a village background, peasant background, my parents were farmers, and I came to love farming when I was a boy, so I studied agriculture and agriculture was my second love after my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were you doing in politics?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, men make mistakes. I made that mistake in 1990 when I thought that by a multi-party system, we would finally rid ourselves of the fetters, and my friends, in view of the position I held in my environment, persuaded me to enter into politics. Right at the beginning, my wife tried to dissuade me and said "Why do you want to go into politics, Slavko. We have a nice life. It's not for you." Unfortunately, I did not listen to her and that's why I find myself here in The Hague today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we see the tape now, please, 13, 14, the 13-14 segments. This is the exit from Vukovar and the road to Ovcara. What part of Vukovar is this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is part of the barracks, it is the Jewish cemetery which had a wall around it when I was President of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now please pay attention to what we are going to see now. What road is this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is the road leading from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that the road you took on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is the road towards Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it is the road that you went along on the 20th of November moving out of Vukovar. Are there any houses there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there are just fields. This is private property all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Stop one minute. This is the turning to Ovcara. From Ovcara to Vukovar, is there a single house?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, there was not a single house on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all we need the tape for. I should now like to ask Your Honours, Mr. Dokmanovic wanted to say a few words, if he may and if that is usual, if it is acceptable? Thank you. And we have no further questions on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Honourable Mr. President, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. After several months, it was eleven months yesterday since I have been in prison, this is the first occasion I have had to say something, for you to hear my voice, the sound of my voice, and I'm very grateful to you for that. As I am under oath, everything that I am going to say will be the truth, and these sentences, including the sentences that I'm addressing to you, esteemed Judges. I thank you very much for the way in which you have conducted my hearing conscientiously. I should like to emphasise the very humane relationship which everybody working, all the staff of the prison have towards me, particularly the warden, Mr. McFadden, who had a lot of understanding for all my human crises. Your Honours, you will bring in a sentence according to your consciences. Whatever that sentence is, you should know that you have a completely broken man sitting before you whose life will never be the same. It is quite certain that this hearing has affected my psyche so much that I don't think I'll ever be able to feel differently than I feel at this moment. Please allow me to say this before I begin to answer any further questions. Please understand that you have before you a man who, under oath, has declared that he has never killed anybody or mistreated anybody in his life. Thank you for hearing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dokmanovic. Mr. Niemann or Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly, there's one sort of housekeeping matter before I start putting questions to Mr. Dokmanovic. In preparing for cross-examination, we realised that the transcript of the interview with Mr. Dokmanovic at the prison omitted the last two pages. The videotape has been provided to the Defence, they were present for the interview, and this is something that we have just discovered. It's a very brief part, but apparently there was discussion about closing the interview out and then it was decided that it would go on and one or two more questions were put to him, so it is on the videotape, it just does not appear in the transcript. I have gotten the transcript done overnight and I have a draft translation of it, so it is not a final translation, but I can supplement this to the transcript that everyone already has or I can give you a new transcript which is complete and encompasses everything. So whatever is your preference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You can simply supplement to the present transcript we already have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, very brief. It's about two pages altogether, so I would mark that as -- it is already marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 128A, this would be 128B, and the version in 128C would be the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, it is the interview that I also attended at the prison; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct. This is the one the Defence was present for and they have received a videotape of it. As I say, there was discussion at the very end about terminating it and then it was decided to go on and ask a couple more questions, and apparently the person transcribing it heard the discussion on concluding it and felt that that was the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dokmanovic, when you met with Mr. Curtis last June in Sombor, you did so with the purpose of talking about crimes committed by Croats against Serbs, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I met him, my intention was to discuss all the crimes that were committed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And during --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not spelled out precisely that we would discuss crimes that were committed by Croats only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And during the course of that interview, you did not offer any information, however, about crimes committed by Serbs, did you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We hadn't even reached that point yet. Our conversation took two days. On the second day, it was very short because Mr. Curtis had actually discharged his task to get me to come to Vukovar. That is why he came to see me, not in order to obtain information. The second day we talked very briefly, and our conversation ended with the 2nd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And when you were discussing the 2nd of May of 1991, the day of the Borovo Selo incident, the version that you gave him was quite different from the view that you expressed in court yesterday, that it was impossible to ascertain who was responsible because, in fact, you told Mr. Curtis that the Croats were exclusively responsible for everything that had happened at Borovo Selo, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that I asked Mr. Ante Markovic and Mr. Manolic, as the Prime Ministers of the Federal and Croatian governments respectively, to ascertain who was guilty for what had happened in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But I believe you also told the court that it was impossible to decide who was responsible.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say it was impossible to ascertain that. It was possible to ascertain it, but I did not have the possibilities to ascertain that or the municipality didn't have the opportunity to ascertain that. Someone who had far greater powers than I did or that the assembly did could only ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But when you spoke with Mr. Curtis, you had very clear views on who was responsible and you expressed those to him, which seems to be different from what you're saying to the court now.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Curtis had the intention of putting me into prison from the very outset. I don't know what he wrote about. I am telling you what it was like. The conflict there was initiated by the Croatian police, but it is certain that not only one side is to be blamed because there was a general showdown, so that is what I was saying on that occasion too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And when you were talking yesterday about offering to voluntarily come to The Hague, that was said in the context of coming here as a witness against Croatian perpetrators, was it not? It was not to come here and stand trial.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No mention was made of the conditions under which I would come to The Hague. We only talked about it, and Mr. Curtis asked me whether I would make a statement and sign a statement or possibly come to The Hague. I said that I would agree to both one and the other. No mention was made of whether it would be under one set of conditions or another set of conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about your family having been in Trpinja for 250 years and how you had been forced from your home. In 1991, by UN estimates, 97 percent of the Croatian population in Vukovar municipality were forced out, and many of those families had been there for 250 years or more. What did you do, as someone who was in and out of political office up until 1996, to bring those people back to their homes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I had a political office until the 6th of June, 1991. What I did after that was not a political office. This was a professional job I did as Minister of Agriculture in the government of the district of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and the director of the Vinarija. When I became President of the Municipal Assembly again in 1994, I advocated the restoration of Vukovar and the signing of the Erdut agreement which meant that everyone should return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In terms of the Erdut agreement, that didn't come about until 1995, did it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when it was signed, when the Erdut agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And, in fact, negotiations for the Erdut agreement did not begin until late 1995 either, did they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And at that point in time, Croatia had just taken back all of the other Serb-held territory within its borders, and so there was a threat of military invasion from Croatia, and Belgrade had made it very clear to the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia that you had to come to some type of agreement with the Croats, had they not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The instructions that I had and the information that I had -- I don't know about what you're saying -- but the group of people who were there decided to go into negotiations. No one ever called me and ordered me to start negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, what I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Dokmanovic, is that at the end of 1995, the people in Eastern Slavonia really did not have much of a choice, and your only option was to enter into negotiations at that point in time, and that the only thing at issue was how long the transition would take and the terms of the transition; isn't that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: From this time distance and from your position, one could think along those lines. At that time and from the position that I was in and the position from which the people were in, those who were in favour of negotiations were a minority even then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, do you recall telling Mr. Curtis on June 24th of last year that in 1991, objectively, there was no way that the Croats could ever come back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. In 1991? What period of 1991? The Croats were in Vukovar in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After the battle had ended in November of 1991, when you were discussing that period with Mr. Curtis, do you recall telling him that objectively the conclusion of you and the government was that there was no way that the Croats could ever come back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that to Mr. Curtis. But, in 1991, after the fighting for Vukovar, there were no proper living conditions for the Croat or the Serb population. There were several thousand inhabitants there, 2.000 or 3.000, in the facilities and the buildings that were preserved at least up to a point, but the rest of the population was either in Serbia or in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, what led you to go to this meeting that was supposed to occur with General Klein was the fact that you were seeking compensation for your house since you had had to leave Croatia. Did your government make any efforts to compensate all of the Croats for the homes that they had lost?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not only my house, it was other houses too, of Serbs who had abandoned that area. That was supposed to be the subject of this discussion, and that is why Mr. Knezevic went with me, who was from Baranja and who also left his house there, so that we could see whether something could be done because all of us who had left did not really have proper homes. But regardless of how I went and why I went, I had full guarantees, both of Mr. Curtis and of Mr. Klein, that I would safely return to Sombor. They both lied. All of that was with the objective of baiting me, bringing me here in a most deceitful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'll again put the question to you: Were any efforts made, while you were in the government or while you were in the municipal administration, to compensate the Croats for their homes that were all destroyed? I mean, your home is still standing in Trpinja. Their homes were levelled. Were any efforts made to compensate them for those houses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: While I was President of the Municipal Assembly in '94 and 1995, restoration works were being carried out on all the buildings, depending on the amount of funds available. The town of Vukovar was so devastated that the municipality did not have the possibility to restore everything that had been destroyed. We talked about that to the members of the European Community and the United Nations and UNTAES, that funds would have to be provided for restoring all of this, and if this would not be done, the renewal of Vukovar would take a very long period of time. No difference was being made when a building was being restored as to whether it was a Serb or a Croat apartment that was being restored. I don't know what you mean when you say that the municipality as an institution should compensate the Croats whose houses were destroyed. There weren't financial resources available for that kind of thing. It wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, if you were a man of peace and reconciliation, why is the perception of you so different among Croats? I mean, you're charged with fomenting rebellion, and you're clearly not welcome in Croatia. Why is that if you were reaching out to them for reconciliation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday evidence was presented here as to what the President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar did in order to preserve the peace in town. If that is not understood, it can be shown once again. But the situation was such that the control and the possibility that the President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar had were not sufficient for preserving the peace. The Croats accuse me because they think that, in a way, I supported the Serb side as President rather than the Croat side. The Serbs are charging me with the opposite, that I was too inclined towards the Croats and that I pursued too lenient a policy, if that was a policy at all. My orientation was to preserve Yugoslavia as much as possible and to have the problems that were coming out resolved by peaceful means. This is highlighted practically in all the statements that were issued. I thought that we were too small an environment to decide on the ultimate outcome of the Yugoslav crisis. I believe until the present day that this should have been resolved at higher levels, not allow every village and every municipality fend for itself to the best of its ability. Regrettably, Vukovar had the toughest time of all. Now, from this time distance, one can lecture what should have been done at that point, but at that time, I was in favour of peace and I clearly expressed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated yesterday that you were present at the meeting in Srb on July 25th, 1990, at the time that the Serb National Council was formed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you said that you were surprised by what you heard there and that, in effect, you disagreed with the views that were being expressed; no?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that. I said that I was surprised by the atmosphere that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, in what way were you surprised?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of Vukovar, we still had a relatively peaceful situation at that time except that the members of the Croatian Democratic Union from time to time demonstrated with cars or in other ways in town and in the surrounding villages, and they flew their national flag, their party flag, they sang provocative songs, and very often they were provoking people in other ways too. At that time, the Serbs were not doing that. When I went there, I saw a big gathering with a lot of Serb insignia and a different kind of atmosphere, something that did not exist in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you viewed this atmosphere in a negative way?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said that I was surprised by what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So were you happy to be offered membership in this organisation, in the Serb National Council?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I was surprised to have been proposed there, and in terms of my inner feelings, I cannot speak of that now, and I think that what I did after that clearly demonstrates what my intention was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking about your inner feelings at that time. Was this something you were in favour of, of joining the organisation or no?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: My political convictions were Yugoslav. I said that several times. It is only on the basis that -- of something that led to Yugoslavia could I emphasise my feelings. You're asking me how I felt seven years ago at that gathering. I cannot tell you precisely. I do not know exactly how I felt. I just know that I was surprised. That is the only thing I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, if you were pro-Yugoslav, why did you just not decline membership in this organisation that was clearly proposing a separatist pact for Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, that is not true. Croatia advocated separatism from Yugoslavia, the Serbs wanted to remain in Yugoslavia; therefore, that problem should be viewed the way it really was, not in a lopsided manner the way you interpret it. As far as my presentation is concerned, that was impossible. I was about -- there were thousands of people, and I was about a hundred metres away from the stage, so it would have been impossible for me to speak out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But you didn't have to join the organisation. I mean, they were creating a Serb National Council, a Serb parliament situated at Srb. This wasn't Yugoslav, this was Serb.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the Serbs in Knin and in other places advocated Yugoslavia, most of them, at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So the way that you viewed this then is that Serbs were basically equal to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is what you're saying. I am saying that the Serb people advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia. Most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, can you understand how this might engender opposition from Croats and Slovenes if you were defining Yugoslavia as an entity which executes the goals of the Serbs and the objectives of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. Yugoslavia existed then as a sovereign state. Separatism from Yugoslavia was being expressed by Slovenia and Croatia. They were the first to do so. Later on, other members did that as well. So this is separatism of the republics that wanted to leave Yugoslavia. And that is the core of the matter. Whether someone was threatened in Yugoslavia or would have been threatened had Yugoslavia remained is another story altogether. Until 1990, I claim that not a single nation or nationality were threatened or endangered in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, this meeting of the Serb National Council, though, where a Serb parliament is set up and a declaration on sovereignty and autonomy of the Serbian people is issued, this occurs eleven months before Croatia declared its independence; correct? Eleven months to the day.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: You have to look at what happened that day in the parliament of the Republic of Croatia and then we can discuss this. Since you have all these documents, you should have documents from the other side as well. That is one thing. Secondly, the Serb people in Croatia were a sovereign people like the Croatian people, and Croatia was a state of the Croatian and Serb peoples, so the equality of rights of these peoples was stipulated in the constitution of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After you became a member of the Serb National Council, you waited until there was criticism from the Croatian side before you resigned at this meeting of the assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated yesterday that there was a tremendous amount of press coverage and that the HDZ had been very critical of you in the press for joining the Serb National Council and that they had called for a meeting of the assembly in which you would be censured, and it was at that point that you resigned. So I'm asking you: Why didn't you resign earlier than that if you had some disagreement with the Serb National Council? Why did you wait until there was criticism from the other side before you acted?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: As regards his work and what he did, the President reported at sessions of the assembly. What happened at that point in time was reported on the next day. And within two or three days, different kinds of criticism were levelled. And within the time framework allowed, I convened the assembly. I cannot convene an assembly meeting on the phone. Invitations had to be issued. So although this was an extraordinary meeting of the assembly, it still took a bit of time to organise it, to convene it, and also to send in all the papers, as was done when regular sessions of the assembly were held too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And it was necessary for you to do this in front of the assembly? You couldn't have gone down to the newspaper or the radio station in Vukovar the day you got back and said, "Yes, this has been reported. I'm resigning immediately"? Why was it necessary to do this in front of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that I went there was publicly announced because at that time I was a member of the Municipal Assembly and I wished to inform the other members of the assembly so that they would be informed and that a solution would be found in that way. Why I did it that way and not go to the radio station and broadcast this; I thought at that time that this was the right way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you actually resign from the Serb National Council or was this just done for public consumption, as Mr. Petrovic says in his history of the council?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: All the media reported on my leaving the Serb National Council, and I said yesterday that I did not take part in the work of a single session of this council, and I don't know whether any sessions were held, nor am I informed in any way as to what the Serb National Council did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What about participating in this meeting in Belgrade that Mr. Petrovic reports in his book where he states that you argued that there should be a separate Serb National Council for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem; was this true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that that is what is written in Mr. Petrovic's book. If you read it out to me, perhaps I could comment on it because I only took a superficial glance at the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. I would ask that this exhibit be brought out -- I'll have to check the number. I believe it's 196. It's going to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, may I just ask that the former assertion made by the Prosecutor, that Petrovic'S book states that he only formally resigned. Would you read out both passages?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm happy to put both of them to him exactly. There were translations -- for the assistance of the Registrar, it could be anywhere between 196 and 202. So if I could perhaps see all of those exhibits and I'll obtain the correct one? Mr. Bos, we have a copy over here, so perhaps I can look through it just a moment and find exactly which ones I'm talking about. Well, the quote in relation to you leaving the Serb National Council in Knin, this appears in Exhibit 196A. Perhaps this can be shown to Mr. Dokmanovic? I believe this is on page 40 of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And this is about midway down in the first paragraph, Mr. Dokmanovic, right before the reference to Mr. Dzakula from Pakrac, and it says --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. What page did you say that was on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's on page 40.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And about halfway down, it says: "The latter two are not members of the council," talking of Caslav Ocic and Slavko Dokmanovic. "However, Dokmanovic still considers himself a member of the council in Knin despite the fact that he left it because of the public." You would disagree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I did not take part in the work of the Serbian National Council and I am repeating this for the third or fourth time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And then a couple of pages later, where it is talking about discussions for setting up another Serb National Council, it says: "After a long argument about the words 'board' and 'committee' and after, at a unpropitious moment, Dokmanovic started insisting on the differences between Vukovar and Knin. Babic finally agreed to the Serb National Council of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem being renamed the Regional Board of the Serbian National Council." But it's your testimony that you were not even present at this meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection, please. The Prosecutor, a moment ago, said that Dokmanovic was in favour of creating the Serbian National Council. That quotation was about Babic. I don't know who Babic is until you bring him here. The Prosecutor is duty-bound to read where that is stated in Petrovic's book, that Dokmanovic advocated the creation of the Serbian National Council, because that is what he said. Can we look at the transcript? May we have a look and see what he said? If there is a quotation of that kind, please let him supply us with it. If not, may we go on to the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought that this was a fair paraphrasing of what it said in the book. I put it to Mr. Dokmanovic. He has indicated that he wasn't even present at the meeting. So I'll accept his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: One other objection. He did not paraphrase, he maintained. Paraphrasing is when you retell something. But Mr. Williamson, the Prosecutor, maintained that Dokmanovic advocated the formation of the Serbian National Council for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. That is not a paraphrase, it is an assertion, and that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might? The question was put to Mr. Dokmanovic. He said that that was not fair, what I had said, and then he denied even being there. All I can do is put questions to him, and I think it's fair cross-examination to ask him certain things and it's up to him to answer it. I mean, he answered it, and he --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, but in the cross-examination, you cannot raise incorrect questions, incorrect assertions, in order to get an answer which provides the possibility for a subsequent question. So will the Prosecutor state that he has quoted incorrectly and then everything will be all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: He did not quote, actually, there was not a quotation. At your request, the two citations were read out, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But he did not quote what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, it was not a citation, he calls it a paraphrase of what the book by Petrovic says. But I think the question has become moot because, in any case, we have the answer from the witness who said that he was not even there. So let us now stop here. You can move on. However, please, Mr. Williamson, whenever you make a statement or you attribute a statement to a book, a document, could you please read out the relevant passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Certainly. I will be happy to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, if you were not present at this meeting, why would --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought I had understood you to say that you weren't there. You were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you discussed and exactly what you proposed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but quite certainly it is not what Ilija Petrovic has written. I was not along the same course as Ilija Petrovic, of the same orientation. And I was invited to go there, I did not know who would be at the meeting, at the Association of Serbs from Croatia, because already at that time a large number of Serbs had begun to leave Croatia, principally from the large towns, and went in the direction of Serbia toward Belgrade and would contact the Association of Serbs from Croatia asking aid and assistance in the solution of their problems, and some political topics cropped up there which Ilija Petrovic is now retelling. Ilija Petrovic lived in Novi Sad. I lived in Vukovar. That is the same as if I had proposed solutions for what should be done in Novi Sad while living in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, going to this book, it's very clear that Mr. Petrovic is quite proud of the Serb National Council and what it accomplished. I mean, he treats it almost like it's his child. It's pretty clear that he doesn't like you and doesn't have a very good opinion of you, so why would he possibly want to give you a bigger role and involvement in the council than you actually had?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what council you're talking about now. If you're talking about the council that Ilija Petrovic considers to be his own baby, that is to say, the Serbian Council of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, I was not a member of that council and had no role there, either large or small.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that in the period between May and June 1991, you were stopped a number of times, taken out of your car, and searched. How many times did this happen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sixty-three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you were taken out at gun point?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those who stopped me were very frequently armed, which was unusual for the police, with long weapons, which was unusual for the police who were there to keep law and order, to use long arms, long rifles in moving about town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And this must have made you extremely angry, did it not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not angry. My esteem was hurt. It was humiliating for the President of the Municipal Assembly to be stopped in the centre of town, to be made to leave his car, to be made to place his hands on the car, and to search him in front of a crowd of people looking at this. That way of work had a very clear message. If they were able to behave like that towards the President of the Municipal Assembly, what could other citizens expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But you weren't angry about this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was humiliated, offended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But not angry?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why do you insist? If I have given you an answer, I have given you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, you indicated yesterday that you got quite angry when the soldier wouldn't let you pass at Orolik and had pointed a gun at you. You said you became very angry. I'm just asking what's different about this? This seems like actually a worse situation and that it would be natural for you to get very angry about someone dragging you out of your car at gun point.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I was offended by the way in which the soldier reacted. He said, "Who fucks you and who fucks the government?" So I was offended with his behaviour, with his conduct. I don't remember saying that I was angry. It is quite usual that I was not in a good mood at the answer of this whipper-snapper to a serious man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, is it true that you travelled to work for some time in an armoured personnel carrier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not true that I went to work in an armoured personnel carrier. They brought me from work in an armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And there were three other armoured personnel carriers escorting you, were there not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact number. I think there were two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And these were provided by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In the period between July and September 1991, you said that you had helped with the wheat harvest around Trpinja and that you had to take it across the Danube by boat because there were Croatian police checkpoints on the bridges; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The roads were blocked. The only communication left open and via which we could reach other parts of the world was via the Danube, to Yugoslavia, to Vojvodina, Serbia. Vukovar was closed off by the members of the police and armed members of the Croatian Democratic Union, and we could not transport the wheat in silos to Vukovar. The only way to save what could have been saved was to go -- to use the Danube. We had no access to any town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But you don't have to pass through Vukovar to go to Erdut and the Erdut bridge from Trpinja, do you? My question is: Why was it necessary to go in boats? Why did you not cross over a bridge into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Which bridge? When I said that everything was controlled by the Croatian side, tell me which bridge I could have used. Perhaps you know the area better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, you just indicated that you could not go into Vukovar. But there's not a bridge in Vukovar, there is a bridge in Erdut, and I'm putting it to you that it was possible for you to get from Trpinja to Erdut without going through Vukovar, and I'm just asking -- I'm just trying to clarify why it was impossible to use the bridges at that time and why it was necessary to go by boat.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The bridge in Erdut was controlled by the Croatian forces and no passage was possible across it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So it was at that time impossible to cross out of Croatia into Serbia without going through a Croatian checkpoint; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not a checkpoint, it was more of a barricade, I would say, which prevented passage. It was not an ordinary checkpoint where you would show your documents and then were able to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But there was a Croatian position on the Croatian side of the bridge which prevented you from crossing into Serbia, be it a checkpoint or a barricade or whatever.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The bridge was blocked by the Croatian police and armed members of the Croatian Democratic Union, and it was not passable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How did it come about that you joined the government of the Serbian district?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I was proposed by the Prime Minister designate, Mr. Hadzic, for Minister of Agriculture, for the post of Minister of Agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, when you spoke with Mr. Milner in the interview at the prison, you seemed to be somewhat reluctant to talk about the fact that you were Minister of Agriculture. He asked you what was your position, and he said "Minister," and then you just said, "I was in charge of agricultural affairs." This is indicated on page 77 of the English transcript. Was there a reason for this? And I can read it out to you verbatim, if you wish. It says, "Listen. I've got to say this. We've got to be honest and forthright here. You were, I think, Minister of Agriculture for a while for the area; is that right?" You replied: "I was in charge of agricultural affairs." He then asked: "What is the title? The person in charge of agricultural affairs?" And then he moves on to another question. But you never reply. Was there a reason why you were reluctant to indicate that you were a Minister in the government?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The function that I performed had no traits, features of Minister. The job that I did was the job of a sort of assistant, at the level of an assistant. So none of the Ministers, in fact, had the competencies or did the title of Minister correspond to the actual jobs they did, and that is why I said that this has nothing to do with Minister. "Minister" is a big title, a big word. What I did was to help people. First of all, to help the peasants, the farmers, because they were the most numerous. As far as possible, to save their harvest, their crops, and to sow new crops, new surface areas with crops, with wheat, and that was my basic job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, we've seen the Defence Exhibit -- I'm not sure of the number offhand -- where it lists you and names you, in fact, as someone who was holding the position of Minister of Agriculture, and at all of the government meetings where we've seen the minutes from, you're referred to as "Minister." So, I mean, why was there a reluctance to say this to Mr. Milner?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that is essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection. The accused has never said that he was reluctant to tell Mr. Milner. Had he not wanted to say this to Mr. Milner, we wouldn't have talked to Mr. Milner. Nobody beat Mr. Dokmanovic and made him talk to Mr. Milner. So do not quote incorrectly that he did not wish to talk to Mr. Milner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, sorry, but Mr. Williamson did not say that the accused had said that he was reluctant to talk to Mr. Milner, he's just asking whether he was reluctant. So it's for the witness to say "Yes" or "No," "I was reluctant," "I was not reluctant," and to explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then there's a change in the translation. All right. Very well. Sorry. I apologise. The translation was, what I heard, that he said that he did not want to speak, and that is not true, that he did not want to talk to Mr. Milner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you rephrase your question and then we will move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I was taking it from what was stated in the interview. These questions were put to you and he asked you specifically, "Were you Minister of Agriculture?" And you said, "No, I was in charge of agricultural affairs." My question to you is: Why were you reluctant to say "I was Minister"? What was the problem in indicating that you were a Minister?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that it was something -- a matter that the Defence would not wish to have that I was a Minister in the government and that everybody who was in the government called themselves Ministers. Those were the way in which the jobs were divided up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How often did you meet with other members of the government?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: With some, more frequently; with some, less frequently. Not all the Ministers were in the same place. There wasn't enough space for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How often were military officers present at meetings of the government?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Very rarely. I don't recall them ever having been present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you go to Erdut on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I went to Erdut every day, almost every day. I can't quite tell you precisely in those four months whether I was prevented from going two or three times in the course of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And did you encounter military checkpoints en route from Trpinja to Erdut?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Several checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And from your testimony this morning, it seems that wearing this hunting uniform that you had, that it helped you to pass through these checkpoints; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those who were at the checkpoints had a greater aversion -- that was my impression -- towards civilians than they did if somebody was dressed similar to them, so to speak. But I explained why I wore the clothing I wore, and I see no reason to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, members of the Territorial Defence and paramilitary groups wore any mixture of uniforms, did they not? We've seen this videotape from VELEPROMET. There is quite a variety of uniforms present there, many of which the JNA officer yesterday did not recognise.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Everybody wore what they had, I suppose. It was wartime. Don't look at the situation from these positions when you can change your tie and suit -- your shirt and suit every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But, in fact, you found it helpful to wear the uniform as well, not only for reasons of not having water, not having electricity, but you found it helpful when you encountered military personnel at checkpoints because they viewed you as someone who was in the military and not as a civilian; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we all wore military uniforms in this courtroom and you were wearing a suit, shirt, and tie, who would be the odd man out? I have explained to you, those were the times, and I have explained why that was the case. The first reason was that it was easy to maintain. It was very difficult to put on a clean shirt every morning, and it was not -- it was out of context because this region was cut off from the world. There was no large town to rely upon for supplies. People had nothing to eat. So this would have been out of place. How could you wear a suit and tie under conditions of this kind? This would lead to great aversion with those who find themselves in a very difficult situation. The second point, the second reason is that there were thousands of refugees in the area that were made to leave Vinkovci and Osijek and other towns in Croatia, and these people came wearing what they had, what they were wearing or what they got, what they received. So I could not behave in a way as in -- and dress with a tie and suit because I had a tie and suit whereas they were mostly wearing sweaters and trousers. You're looking at this from the wrong angle of vision, from the wrong aspect, from a position which is far removed from wartime and in a space of time seven years later, and you're trying to impart -- say that I wore this to show that I was a great soldier or something else of the kind. Yesterday we were shown exhibits that I was not mobilised, and today I state again that I wore what I was able to wear, what was at hand at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, the uniform that you have indicated was yours, this Defence Exhibit 48, when and where did you purchase this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. And is it vital? It is my personal property. I did not receive it from the army or the paramilitary, as you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Territorial Defence during the war in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, on the flight back to The Hague after your arrest, I asked you if you were part of the Territorial Defence, and you initially said "No." You then added, and I quote: "Everyone was with the Territorial Defence during war operations but just in my village where I lived." I then asked you your rank in the Territorial Defence and you said "None." This appears at page 21, 22 of the transcript from the interview on the aeroplane, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 127. So I would ask you now, Mr. Dokmanovic, what you said on the aeroplane then was incorrect? That's 127A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you please read what you are saying? Your Honour, you drew the Prosecutor's attention to reading when he was saying something. So don't do it from your head, please read the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, just read out the passage which is on the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But he must give Mr. Dokmanovic a copy to see what is being read. That is the essential point. Dokmanovic must be able to see what he is reading from. Is that a lot to ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So, Mr. Williamson, could you please tell the witness on what page of the transcript this passage --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. This appears on page 21, and it's about halfway down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And I put the question to Mr. Dokmanovic: "Did you do service with the Territorial Defence or in the Yugoslav Reserve Forces?" The response was "No." I then said "Never"? He said "Never." And then Mr. Dokmanovic volunteered: "Everyone was with the Territorial Defence during war operations, but just in my village where I -- where I lived." And I then asked: "What was your rank in the Territorial Defence?" And you said "None."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a fair question to Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, it's okay. I have no objection to the validity of the question. That is not what I wanted to say. I should like to ask that it be read out in Serbian as well. During the war -- this is the text in Serbian. It has been translated here that -- I would like that passage to be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this appears both in Serbian and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There is the word "with," "'with' the Territorial Defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At any point where it's in Serbian, it was also translated so that there was an exact translation into English of what he said, not relying on what the translator had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, have you found the relevant passage, the passage which we are discussing now in the transcript which is in front of you? Yes? Could you please read it out in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: "During the war operations, everybody was the Territorial Defence, but only in my village where I lived."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please go on? "Only my village where I lived." And ...

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: "What was your rank in the Territorial Defence?" "No rank."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now answer the questions put by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Certainly. You initially said "No," that you weren't in the Territorial Defence, and then you volunteered this information that everyone was in the Territorial Defence, everyone was mobilised, you said "Just in my village." Why did you add this, that you were in the Territorial Defence but just in your village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Every village was organised -- organised its defence, the defence of the village, and there were moments when there was a threat of danger from attack by Croatian forces in my village. My village was very close to Vukovar, and the village was closed off then and nobody could leave the village. None of the men. And at that time -- that is what I had in mind. At that time, we were all members of the village's defence, not the formation of Territorial Defence. Just the defence of the village, in defending the village, not as Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, I just have a couple of more questions, Your Honour, and then perhaps we can take a break -- a couple of questions before the break. I'll have some afterward as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During 1991, did you ever wear any other type of military uniform, perhaps a JNA reserve officer's uniform?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: After 1991 or before -- when? When? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During 1991, at any point.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I wore what has been displayed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You don't recall wearing a JNA reserve officer's uniform in Trpinja in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In August 1991? I don't recall. But I do not preclude that possibility if those were the orders of the commander of the defence of the village, that everyone should wear a military uniform. Perhaps that could have happened. I do not recall that it happened, but perhaps it could have happened one day. But I did not wear a military uniform. Perhaps there were orders to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So you were in some type of organisation where you were subject to orders, and when you received these orders, you'd put on a military uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that every village had a defence staff for defending the village, and the decisions of that staff had to be observed. I had no role there whatsoever except for an ordinary citizen, except that of an ordinary citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you're saying you don't recall, but there is the possibility that you might have had on a uniform during this period, a reserve officer's uniform?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I never had the uniform of a reserve officer. I never said that, and please don't put words into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well, that was the question that I asked you, and you said that there was a possibility. My question exactly was: "You don't recall wearing a JNA reserve officer's uniform in Trpinja in August of 1991?" Your answer was: "In August 1991? I don't recall. But I do not preclude that possibility if those were the orders of the commander of the village." So I'm not putting words into your mouth. That was the direct question I asked you and that was your response.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was never a reserve officer nor did I ever have the uniform of a reserve officer. Please, that is quite clear, and that has been said several times. So why do you insist all the time when there is less attention on my part and you're trying to put words into my mouth? I never said that I wore a reserve officer's uniform because I never was a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, I'm not trying to put words in your mouth. I quoted that. If you misunderstood me or you weren't clear on what I was saying, you should let me know, but I'm quoting directly what you said. I'm not trying to put words in your mouth. Did you wear any other uniform other than this hunting uniform at any time, and if so, what kind of uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall, but I do not preclude the possibility that there were orders, if there was a threat of danger, and if that was the assessment of the defence of the village, that there was danger of attack, that we should all come there and put on uniforms. According to the previous rules and regulations of the JNA, all members of the reserve had JNA uniforms at home, which they kept at home. Not in 1990. My uniform of a reserve soldier I obtained when I came back after having done my regular military service, so it is possible that I could have obtained it sometime in 1976, 1977, or 1978. So I kept it at home, and everyone's duty was to do that. But now I cannot recall -- I don't think so, but I cannot say for sure 100 percent whether something like that happened because at that time there were -- there was danger, and the Croatian side tried to attack the village or there was a threat of that kind of danger of that having happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we could take the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I did not want to interrupt Mr. Williamson, so I didn't want to influence the answers of the witness, but since you now said that we are on break, perhaps I could explain why there's this misunderstanding? When Mr. Williamson asked whether he wore a uniform of the reserve officer, this was part of the transcript. But it was translated into the Serb language whether he wore the uniform of a reservist, not a reserve officer. So the officer, the word "officer" disappeared in the Serbian translation, and that is the source of this misunderstanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, when you went to Ilok on October 16th of 1991, did you go to a meeting where Professor Magovac was present as one of the negotiators for the people of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone isn't on. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat what you said, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not one of the negotiators. I simply happened to see Magovac there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But you did go to the meeting? You were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not a meeting. I was present. I told you why I went there and that is where I saw Mr. Magovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you recall telling Mr. Magovac that peoples courts would be set up at the end of all of this to determine who was guilty?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I never said that, nor was it within my competence to set up any kind of courts. I told Mr. Magovac then -- I mean, I asked him, "Why are you doing that?" Something to that effect. And he said it was decided that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you asked him, "Why are you doing that?" what were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I meant, why was such great tensions being created that lead to such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And it was your belief that this was the fault of the Croats, if you were asking Professor Magovac, "Why are you doing that?"

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say, "Why are you doing that?" I said, "Why are you doing that?" And I didn't say it was only -- I wasn't saying that it was only the fault of the Croats. There were people to be blamed on all sides. But when I was talking to him, why could I ask him why somebody else was doing it? I was saying this to him because I was talking to him. But I never mentioned any kind of peoples courts. I said that this was not within my competence. At that time I was involved in organising agriculture, and I did not have any reason to mention this, nor would I have ever mentioned something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But when you addressed Professor Magovac and said "you", were you indicating this in the singular, indicating Mr. Magovac alone as being responsible, or were you indicating "you" in the plural form, meaning a group of people, and if so, what group of people?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the general situation. I knew Mr. Magovac from before. We weren't any great friends, but I think that we would be relatively -- in relatively good relations even today, had the situation been different. So I was saying this as a friend to a friend. I meant well, and I was referring to the general situation, why all of that was happening. I was not blaming any particular side for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you posed this question to him, do you recall him answering you and saying, "Slavko, what did I do?"

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think it was that way. This was a long time ago and this conversation took five minutes, or three minutes. I can't really say. And I think that he said that is the way it was decided. I did not ask him anything more about that. We just shook hands, and he went to one side and I went elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You didn't go to Ilok because you felt it was part of your area of responsibility as the President or past President of Vukovar Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any authority, any powers then. I was no longer performing the duties of the President, and I already said that after the 6th of June I was no longer President, and I didn't behave like President, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you talk regularly with Ljubo Novakovic about what was going on in Ilok, where Mr. Novakovic was briefing you, more or less, as one Municipality President to another?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I was not President. With Ljubo Novakovic I maintained relations which primarily had to do with agricultural affairs. He was in a border municipality, and since he was my acquaintance, I could get certain assistance that was needed at that point in time, that is to say, mechanisation, reproduction materials, but also basic supplies for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On the morning of the 20th of November -- I'm sorry, let me go back just a moment. Strike that. Now, on the 19th of November, what occurred at the government meeting that you attended in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing occurred. It was a regular government meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you had a chance to review the minutes of that meeting yesterday. Did those accurately reflect your recollection of what did occur there and what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I took a look at the minutes and they seemed to be reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What plans were made for the meeting the following day in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no plans were being made. This was a statement made by the Prime Minister that one should go to Vukovar the next day without any plans and without special duties involved for anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you felt it important to be there; did you not? This was the first meeting to be held in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the government. Mr. Hadzic was Prime Minister. Therefore, what the Prime Minister asked individual members to do was something that they were supposed to do. But I said yesterday that I think it was decisive that the members of the delegation from Kladovo wanted to see the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And, once again, can you just tell us what was the purpose of the meeting, the 20th; what was the reason for having the meeting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The fighting around Vukovar was over, and that has been said several times now. Again, you are pre-judging the status of the government here. It was not something that constituted a real government. It was probably an assessment of the Prime Minister that it would be necessary for the members of the government to appear in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On the morning of the 20th of November, what time did you get up?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: As usual, sometime around 7.00, perhaps a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what did you do that morning, before leaving your home in Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably as usual. I did certain things related to my hygiene, and then I had breakfast, and I think that we headed off towards Palanka around 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you remember if you had a shower and a shave like Mr. Cvetkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I didn't know that I would be in The Hague and that I'd have to remember what I did on the morning of the 20th. I probably shaved. I did that regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what time did you leave to go to Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC
